reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: Presents with progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness affecting shoulder and hip girdles, causing difficulty rising from chairs, climbing stairs, and lifting the arms
Weakness rather than pain predominates, and there is no characteristic rash (distinguishing it from dermatomyositis)
Serum creatine kinase is typically markedly elevated, reflecting muscle fibre damage
Myositis-specific antibodies, including the antisynthetase antibodies (e.g. anti-Jo-1), help define clinical subsets
The antisynthetase syndrome combines myositis with interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and 'mechanic's hands'
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; inclusion body myositis in older patients and other myopathies must be considered before labelling weakness as polymyositis
Muscle biopsy classically shows endomysial CD8 T-cell infiltration surrounding and invading non-necrotic fibres
Corticosteroids are the mainstay of initial treatment, with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants added to control disease and limit steroid toxicity
reference.pathophysiology: Polymyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy driven by cell-mediated autoimmunity. Cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes recognise antigens expressed on muscle fibres and invade non-necrotic myofibres, causing fibre necrosis and regeneration and consequent weakness. Upregulation of MHC class I on muscle fibres is characteristic. Associations with specific autoantibodies define distinct phenotypes, and there is overlap with other connective tissue diseases and, less strongly than in dermatomyositis, with malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Endocrine myopathy (hypothyroidism, Cushing) and drug-induced myopathy
Motor neuron disease and myasthenia gravis
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes
Myositis-specific and myositis-associated antibody panel including anti-Jo-1
Electromyography showing a myopathic pattern with irritability
MRI of muscle to identify oedema and guide biopsy
Muscle biopsy for endomysial inflammation; screening for interstitial lung disease with pulmonary function tests and high-resolution CT
redFlags: Rapidly progressive dyspnoea or hypoxia from interstitial lung disease, especially with antisynthetase antibodies
Bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness causing dysphagia, aspiration, or ventilatory compromise
Cardiac involvement with arrhythmia or heart failure
Features suggesting an underlying occult malignancy
reference.prognosis: With treatment many patients regain strength, but relapses are common and prognosis is worse in the presence of interstitial lung disease, cardiac involvement, severe dysphagia, or associated malignancy. Long-term functional outcome depends on early treatment and control of extramuscular disease.
pitfalls: Diagnosing polymyositis without excluding inclusion body myositis and necrotising myopathy, which respond differently to therapy
Overlooking interstitial lung disease, a major cause of morbidity and mortality
Attributing weakness solely to steroid myopathy during treatment without reassessing disease activity
Failing to screen for dysphagia and aspiration risk
Missing an associated malignancy or overlap connective tissue disease
management: High-dose corticosteroids as first-line therapy to suppress the cell-mediated myositis
Early introduction of a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as methotrexate or azathioprine, with intravenous immunoglobulin or rituximab for refractory disease
Treatment of antisynthetase-associated interstitial lung disease with agents such as mycophenolate, ciclosporin or cyclophosphamide
Physiotherapy to preserve and rebuild muscle strength, with speech and language therapy and aspiration precautions for dysphagia
Monitoring of creatine kinase and objective muscle strength to gauge response, with surveillance for interstitial lung and cardiac involvement
Age-appropriate malignancy screening given the association with underlying cancer
Bone protection and Pneumocystis prophylaxis to cover prolonged immunosuppression
Rheumatology-led multidisciplinary care, reconsidering the diagnosis where inclusion body myositis is possible
